chunks: "You'd need more than one controller when two different devices both have to initiate transactions on the same bus.
For instance a main processor and a low-power sensor hub both reading the same sensors, a host and a charger both talking to a battery fuel gauge, or a redundant second MCU for fail-over.
Another case is when a target needs to tell a controller something and you'd rather it send the message than have the controller poll, in which case the target briefly acts as a controller.
I2C supports that through arbitration. If two controllers start at the same moment, they both drive the bus, and because the lines are open-drain, a low always wins.
Each controller watches SDA while it sends.
If one sends a 1, which means it released the line, but sees a 0, someone else is pulling low, so it knows it lost, stops transmitting, and waits for a STOP.
The winner doesn't even notice, because the bit it was sending was never corrupted. The clocks synchronize the same way, since SCL is also wired-AND.
That said, I'd avoid multi-master if I could.
Every controller has to support it, handle arbitration loss, and wait for the bus to be free, and a hung controller can lock the whole bus.
Often an interrupt line, a second bus, or a single controller that owns the bus is simpler and more robust."
